tullamoredew-sb: Tullamore's distillery was founded in 1829 by Michael Molloy in the County Offaly town that gives the whiskey its name. Daniel E. Williams joined as a teenager, rose to run the business and lent it his initials, which inspired the slogan 'Give every man his Dew'. The distillery closed in 1954 and the brand was made elsewhere for decades, until William Grant & Sons bought it in 2010 and opened a new distillery on the edge of Tullamore in 2014, bringing the whiskey home.
tullamoredew12-sb: The 12-year-old Special Reserve is an older bottling of Tullamore D.E.W., whose story begins at a distillery founded in the County Offaly town of Tullamore in 1829. Like the standard blend it is triple distilled and combines pot still, malt and grain whiskeys, here matured in ex-bourbon and oloroso sherry casks for at least twelve years. The D.E.W. stands for Daniel E. Williams, the manager whose initials became the brand's name, and since 2014 the brand has again had a distillery in its home town, owned by William Grant & Sons.
teelingsmallbatch-sb: Jack Teeling founded the Teeling Whiskey Company in 2012, reviving a family name in Dublin distilling that goes back to 1782, when Walter Teeling set up a distillery on Marrowbone Lane. With his brother Stephen he opened a new distillery in the Liberties in 2015, billed as the first new whiskey distillery in Dublin for more than 125 years. Small Batch, one of the company's first releases, is a blend finished in rum casks and bottled at 46 percent without chill filtration, and the phoenix on the label stands for the revival of Dublin distilling.
teelingsinglemalt-sb: The Teeling family's modern whiskey business began in 2012, when Jack Teeling left Cooley, the distillery his father John had founded, after its sale to Beam, and set up on his own in Dublin with a stock of aged whiskey. Teeling Single Malt reflects the house taste for unusual cask finishes, marrying malts finished in five kinds of wine cask: sherry, port, madeira, white burgundy and cabernet sauvignon. The family's new distillery in the Liberties began production in 2015, near the site where Walter Teeling distilled in the eighteenth century.
connemarapeated-sb: Connemara arrived in 1996 from the Cooley Distillery in County Louth, which John Teeling had opened in 1987 in a converted potato alcohol plant. Peated Irish whiskey had all but vanished, and Cooley set out to revive it with a smoky single malt, double rather than triple distilled, in the Scotch manner. The name borrows Connemara, the boggy western corner of County Galway where turf has been cut for generations, although the whiskey is made on the opposite coast. Cooley has belonged to Beam, now Suntory Global Spirits, since 2012.
tyrconnell-sb: The Tyrconnell began as a whiskey of A. A. Watt and Co. of Derry, named after a racehorse owned by Andrew Alexander Watt that won the National Produce Stakes in 1876 at odds of 100 to 1. The brand lay dormant from the 1920s until the Cooley Distillery revived it as a single malt in the early 1990s, keeping the racehorse on the label. Tyrconnell, Tír Chonaill in Irish, is the old name of the O'Donnell territory in what is now County Donegal.
kilbeggan-sb: Kilbeggan's distillery in County Westmeath dates its founding to 1757, when Matthew MacManus began distilling there, and it claims to be the oldest licensed distillery in Ireland, a distinction long debated with Bushmills. The Locke family took it over in 1843 and ran it for more than a century, until production stopped in the 1950s. The Cooley Distillery bought the brand and the old site in the late 1980s, and in 2007, the 250th anniversary, distilling resumed in the stone buildings beside the River Brosna.
writerstears-sb: Writers' Tears comes from Walsh Whiskey, the family company Bernard and Rosemary Walsh founded in County Carlow in 1999 to take part in the revival of Irish whiskey. It blends single pot still and single malt whiskeys with no grain whiskey, a combination the Walshes present as a return to the style Irish writers would have known around the turn of the twentieth century. The name is a playful tribute to Ireland's literary tradition, and the whiskey is triple distilled and matured in American oak.
midletonveryrare-sb: Irish Distillers launched Midleton Very Rare in 1984, nine years after it had gathered its production into the new Midleton Distillery in County Cork. Released once a year as a vintage, it was conceived as the group's prestige blend, drawing on selected older pot still and grain whiskeys, and each bottle carries the signature of the master distiller of the day. Barry Crockett oversaw the early decades of the release, and his successors have kept it going every year since.
roeco-sb: Diageo launched Roe & Co in 2017 as a blended Irish whiskey honouring George Roe, whose family's Thomas Street distillery in Dublin was once among the largest in Britain and Ireland before it closed in 1926. In 2019 the company began distilling at its own Roe & Co distillery in the former Guinness power station on Thomas Street, close to the old Roe site and to St Patrick's Tower, the windmill that once served the Roe distillery and still stands over the street.
slane-sb: Slane whiskey belongs to the Conyngham family's estate at Slane Castle in the Boyne Valley of County Meath, whose grounds are better known for the open-air rock concerts held there for decades. Henry Mount Charles and his son Alex Conyngham first bottled a Slane whiskey from sourced stock, and in 2015 Brown-Forman bought the business and began building a distillery in the castle's old stable yard, which started distilling in 2017. The flagship blend is matured in virgin oak, seasoned oak and oloroso sherry casks, hence its Triple Casked label.
methodandmadness-sb: Irish Distillers introduced Method and Madness in 2017 as an experimental range from the Midleton Distillery in County Cork. The name comes from Hamlet, where Polonius remarks that though this be madness, yet there is method in it. The single pot still bottling is finished in French chestnut casks, a wood rarely used for whiskey, and set the tone for a series built on unusual woods and techniques.
waterfordsinglefarmorigin-sb: Waterford Distillery was founded in 2014 by Mark Reynier, formerly of Bruichladdich on Islay, who bought a modern brewery built by Guinness on the quays of Waterford city and converted it to distilling. His idea was terroir: barley from individual Irish farms, grown on different soils, harvested and distilled separately so that each farm's spirit could be compared. The first Single Farm Origin bottlings appeared in 2020, each named after the farm that grew its barley.
dinglesinglemalt-sb: Dingle Distillery opened on the Dingle Peninsula in County Kerry in 2012, in the old Fitzgerald sawmill on the edge of the town. Its founder was Oliver Hughes, a pioneer of Irish craft brewing through the Porterhouse pubs, who died in 2016. Its single malt is triple distilled in the Irish manner, matured in a mix of casks and released in small batches, and it was among the first whiskeys from the new wave of independent Irish distilleries.
knappoguecastle12-sb: Knappogue Castle whiskey takes its name from a fifteenth-century tower house near Quin in County Clare, once a MacNamara stronghold, which the American Mark Edwin Andrews and his wife Lavonne bought and restored in the twentieth century. The whiskey was created by the Andrews family and is marketed by Castle Brands, now part of Pernod Ricard. It is not made at the castle: the 12-year-old is bottled from sourced, triple-distilled Irish single malt.
banpoitin-sb: Bán, Irish for white or fair, is a modern legal Irish poitín, a spirit named after the small pot, or pota, it was traditionally made in, long distilled illicitly in the countryside and allowed back on the Irish market only at the end of the twentieth century.
madmarchharepoitin-sb: Mad March Hare is a modern, legally made Irish poitín, the traditionally unaged pot still spirit long tied to illicit country distilling, and its name borrows the old phrase mad as a March hare.
makersmark-sb: Bill Samuels Sr. bought the old Burks' Distillery at Star Hill Farm in Loretto, Kentucky, in 1953 and set out to make a softer bourbon, using red winter wheat in place of rye. His wife, Margie Samuels, named it, designed the label and came up with the hand-dipped red wax seal; a collector of pewter, she knew that its makers stamped their work with a maker's mark. The first batch was bottled in 1958, and the wax is still applied by hand at the distillery, which is now part of Suntory Global Spirits.
makersmark46-sb: Maker's 46 arrived in 2010 as the first new bourbon from Maker's Mark since the brand's founding in the 1950s. Bill Samuels Jr., then running the company his parents had started, worked with the Independent Stave Company on a finish that would build on the house flavour: fully matured Maker's Mark is finished with seared French oak staves fixed inside the barrel. The name is usually explained as the number of the stave profile chosen in the trials. Like the original, it is a wheated bourbon made at Loretto, Kentucky.
makersmarkcaskstrength-sb: Maker's Mark Cask Strength first appeared in 2014 in small quantities at the distillery in Loretto, Kentucky, and later reached a wider market. It is the standard Maker's Mark wheated bourbon bottled straight from the barrel, without the water that brings the regular bottling down to its usual strength, so its proof varies from batch to batch. The brand itself dates from 1953, when Bill Samuels Sr. bought the Star Hill Farm distillery, and every bottle still carries Margie Samuels's dipped red wax.
woodfordreserve-sb: Brown-Forman launched Woodford Reserve in 1996 after restoring an old stone distillery on Glenn's Creek near Versailles, Kentucky, and named it after Woodford County. Distilling on the site goes back to 1812 and Elijah Pepper, and in the nineteenth century James Crow, credited with refining the sour mash method, worked at the Oscar Pepper distillery there. Labrot & Graham owned it from 1878; Brown-Forman bought it in 1941, later sold it and bought it back in 1993, and the distillery is now a National Historic Landmark.
woodfordreservedoubleoaked-sb: Double Oaked joined the Woodford Reserve range in 2012, devised by master distiller Chris Morris. Fully matured Woodford Reserve is moved into a second new barrel that has been deeply toasted before a light charring, and rests there for a further period, drawing extra sweetness and colour from the wood. The brand itself dates from 1996, when Brown-Forman revived the historic distillery on Glenn's Creek in Woodford County, Kentucky, where the Pepper family first distilled in the early nineteenth century.
buffalotrace-sb: Buffalo Trace Kentucky Straight Bourbon was launched in 1999, the year the Sazerac Company renamed its Frankfort distillery after the ancient buffalo trail that crossed the Kentucky River there. The distillery traces distilling on the site to the late eighteenth century, and later owners included E. H. Taylor Jr. and George T. Stagg, whose name it bore for much of the twentieth century. Under Albert Blanton it stayed open through Prohibition, licensed to make whiskey for medicinal use, and it is now a National Historic Landmark.
eaglerare10-sb: Eagle Rare was created for Seagram in 1975 by master distiller Charles L. Beam, and it began as a 101-proof ten-year-old bourbon. The Sazerac Company bought it from Seagram in 1989 and moved production to its Frankfort distillery, now Buffalo Trace, where it is bottled at ten years old and 90 proof. An older sibling, Eagle Rare 17, appears each year in the Buffalo Trace Antique Collection.
blantonssinglebarrel-sb: Blanton's was introduced in 1984 by Elmer T. Lee at the Frankfort distillery that is now Buffalo Trace, and is generally credited as the first modern bourbon marketed as a single barrel. It honours Colonel Albert B. Blanton, who joined the distillery in 1897 at sixteen and was its president from 1921; the story goes that he set aside barrels from a favoured warehouse for friends and guests. Each stopper carries one of eight racehorse and jockey figures, marked with letters that together spell the brand's name.
wellerspecialreserve-sb: William Larue Weller began selling whiskey in Louisville in 1849 and is often credited as the first to make straight bourbon with wheat in place of rye, though the claim rests largely on brand tradition. His firm, W. L. Weller and Sons, later employed a young salesman, Julian 'Pappy' Van Winkle, and after Prohibition it joined the Stitzel distillery to form Stitzel-Weller. The Sazerac Company bought the Weller brand in 1999 and makes it at Buffalo Trace, still with wheat. Special Reserve, with its green label, is the entry point of the range.
wellerantique107-sb: Weller Antique 107 takes its name from its strength, 107 proof, and was long sold as Old Weller Antique with an age statement. The brand descends from William Larue Weller, a Louisville merchant who began selling whiskey in 1849 and is traditionally credited with the wheated bourbon recipe, a style later made famous at the Stitzel-Weller distillery under Julian 'Pappy' Van Winkle. Since 1999 the Sazerac Company has made Weller at Buffalo Trace in Frankfort, and the red-label Antique sits between the gentler Special Reserve and the barrel-proof William Larue Weller.
pappyvanwinkle15-sb: Julian 'Pappy' Van Winkle Sr., who had started out as a travelling salesman for W. L. Weller and Sons, opened the Stitzel-Weller distillery in Louisville in 1935, and wheated bourbon became its house style. After the family sold the distillery in 1972, his son revived the Old Rip Van Winkle label, and his grandson Julian III later built the Family Reserve range that carries Pappy's portrait, cigar in hand. Since 2002 the whiskey has been made with Buffalo Trace, and small releases and long ageing have made it one of the hardest bourbons to find.
vanwinklespecialreserve12-sb: Old Rip Van Winkle was a pre-Prohibition label owned by the Van Winkle family, and after the Stitzel-Weller distillery was sold in 1972, Julian Van Winkle Jr. revived it with aged stocks from the old plant. His son Julian III took over in 1981 and built the range into today's Van Winkle line, which includes this 12-year-old Special Reserve, labelled Lot B. Since 2002 the bourbons, still made to the family's wheated recipe, have been produced in partnership with Buffalo Trace in Frankfort, Kentucky.
georgetstagg-sb: George T. Stagg was first released in 2002 as part of the Buffalo Trace Antique Collection, an uncut and unfiltered bourbon aged for around fifteen years and bottled at whatever strength the barrels give. It honours George T. Stagg, the St Louis whiskey merchant who took over the Frankfort distillery from E. H. Taylor Jr. in 1878, and whose name the distillery carried for much of the twentieth century. The distillery credits Stagg with installing steam heat in its warehouses, an early form of climate-controlled ageing.
bookers-sb: Booker Noe, Jim Beam's grandson and the family's master distiller, liked his bourbon straight from the barrel, uncut and unfiltered, and for years he bottled it that way as gifts for friends, so the story goes. In 1988 the company released it commercially as Booker's, the first of what became the Small Batch Bourbon Collection. Each batch is drawn from barrels roughly six to eight years old and bottled at barrel proof, and Booker's son Fred Noe, now master distiller, continues the line.
bakers7-sb: Baker's was one of the four bourbons in Jim Beam's Small Batch Bourbon Collection, launched in 1992 alongside Booker's, Basil Hayden's and Knob Creek. It is named after Baker Beam, a grandnephew of Jim Beam who spent decades as a distiller at the family's Clermont plant in Kentucky. It is aged seven years and bottled at 107 proof, and since 2019 it has been sold as a single barrel bourbon, each bottle marked with its barrel number.
knobcreek9-sb: Booker Noe created Knob Creek in 1992 for Jim Beam's Small Batch Bourbon Collection, aiming at the fuller, older style of bourbon from before Prohibition. Its name comes from Knob Creek in Kentucky, where Abraham Lincoln's family farmed during his boyhood, and its label borrows the look of a nineteenth-century bottle wrapped in newspaper. Aged nine years and bottled at 100 proof, it lost its age statement for a few years when stocks ran short, then regained it.
knobcreeksinglebarrel-sb: Knob Creek began in 1992, when Booker Noe added it to Jim Beam's Small Batch Bourbon Collection as a full-bodied nine-year-old named after the Kentucky creek where Abraham Lincoln spent part of his boyhood. The Single Barrel Reserve came later, drawn from individual barrels of nine-year-old bourbon and bottled at 120 proof, so each bottling varies with its barrel. Many barrels are chosen by bars and shops through the brand's private barrel programme and bottled under their names.
basilhayden-sb: Basil Hayden was introduced in 1992 as part of Jim Beam's Small Batch Bourbon Collection, a lighter bourbon at 80 proof built on a high-rye recipe. It is named after Basil Hayden Sr., a Catholic settler who led families from Maryland to Nelson County, Kentucky, in the late eighteenth century and is said to have used more rye than usual in his mash. His grandson Raymond Hayden later named the Old Grand-Dad brand in his honour, and the old man's portrait still appears on that label.
jimbeamwhitelabel-sb: The Beam family dates its bourbon to around 1795, when Jacob Beam, a farmer of German descent, sold his first barrels in Kentucky. The family whiskey was sold as Old Tub in the late nineteenth century, and after Prohibition James Beauregard Beam rebuilt the business at Clermont, Kentucky, where the bourbon came to carry his own name. The White Label is aged four years, and the family line continues: Fred Noe, Jim Beam's great-grandson, is the seventh-generation master distiller.
jimbeamblack-sb: Jim Beam Black is the longer-aged companion to the White Label, drawn from the same family recipe but left longer in the barrel and bottled at a higher strength. The family dates its bourbon to about 1795 and Jacob Beam's first barrels in Kentucky; after Prohibition James B. Beam rebuilt the distillery at Clermont, and the bourbon took his name. Black was long sold as an eight-year-old before its age statement changed, and it is still made at Clermont under the family's master distillers.
wildturkey101-sb: Wild Turkey's name comes from 1940, when Thomas McCarthy, an executive of the New York firm Austin Nichols, took some 101-proof bourbon from the company's stock on a wild turkey hunting trip. His friends kept asking for 'that wild turkey bourbon', and Austin Nichols began bottling it under the name in 1942. The whiskey came from the Ripy family's distillery at Lawrenceburg, Kentucky, which Austin Nichols bought in 1971, and Jimmy Russell, who joined in 1954, became its long-serving master distiller.
wildturkeyrarebreed-sb: Jimmy Russell created Rare Breed in 1991 as Wild Turkey's barrel-proof bourbon, originally a marriage of six-, eight- and twelve-year-old stocks bottled without added water. Russell had joined the Lawrenceburg, Kentucky, distillery in 1954 and became master distiller in 1967, and Rare Breed presents the house style at full strength. The brand name itself dates from a 1940 hunting trip, when an Austin Nichols executive shared some of the company's bourbon with friends who kept asking for 'that wild turkey bourbon'.
russellsreserve10-sb: Russell's Reserve was introduced in the early 2000s and named after Wild Turkey's father-and-son distillers, Jimmy and Eddie Russell. Jimmy joined the Lawrenceburg, Kentucky, distillery in 1954 and became master distiller in 1967; Eddie followed him there in 1981 and was named master distiller in 2015. The 10-year-old is a small batch bourbon bottled at 90 proof, a little gentler than the 101-proof Wild Turkey that made the house's name.
fourrosessmallbatch-sb: Paul Jones Jr. filed the Four Roses trademark in 1888, though the brand's origins are disputed and another account credits Rufus Mathewson Rose. The familiar story is a romantic legend: a Southern belle answered Jones's proposal by wearing a corsage of four red roses. Seagram bought Four Roses in 1943 and from the late 1950s sold it as straight bourbon only overseas, offering Americans a blend instead, until Kirin's purchase in 2002 brought the bourbon home. Small Batch marries four of the distillery's ten recipes, built from two mash bills and five yeast strains.
fourrosessinglebarrel-sb: Four Roses traces its trademark to 1888 and Paul Jones Jr., and its Spanish Mission-style distillery near Lawrenceburg, Kentucky, built in 1910, is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The distillery makes ten separate bourbons from two mash bills and five yeast strains, and the Single Barrel bottles just one of them, the high-rye OBSV recipe, at 100 proof. For decades Four Roses straight bourbon was sold only abroad, until Kirin bought the brand in 2002 and reintroduced it in the United States.
elijahcraigsmallbatch-sb: Heaven Hill launched Elijah Craig in 1986 as a twelve-year-old small batch bourbon, and in 2016 it dropped the age statement to stretch its stocks. It is named after the Reverend Elijah Craig, an eighteenth-century Baptist preacher and early Kentucky distiller, whom legend credits with first charring barrels and so inventing bourbon, a story historians do not accept. Heaven Hill, a Bardstown family company founded in 1935, has distilled at the Bernheim distillery in Louisville since 1999, after a 1996 fire destroyed its Bardstown distillery.
elijahcraigbarrelproof-sb: Elijah Craig Barrel Proof was introduced by Heaven Hill in 2013, an uncut and unfiltered version of its Elijah Craig bourbon, usually around twelve years old and released in three batches a year, each with its own proof and a code showing when it came out. The brand began in 1986 and takes its name from the Reverend Elijah Craig, a Baptist preacher and early Kentucky distiller credited by legend, though not by historians, with charring the first bourbon barrels.
evanwilliamsblack-sb: Heaven Hill introduced Evan Williams in 1957, naming it after a Welsh-born settler whom the label credits as Kentucky's first distiller, working on the banks of the Ohio at Louisville in 1783. Historians have questioned both the date and the claim to be first, but the name stuck, and Evan Williams became one of Heaven Hill's leading bourbons. It is distilled at the Bernheim distillery in Louisville, and the Evan Williams Bourbon Experience stands on the city's Whiskey Row.
evanwilliamsbottledinbond-sb: Evan Williams has been a Heaven Hill brand since 1957, named for an eighteenth-century Welsh settler said to have distilled at Louisville. The white-label Bottled-in-Bond follows the Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897, a law passed to guarantee unadulterated whiskey: it must come from one distillery and one distilling season, age at least four years in a federally bonded warehouse and be bottled at 100 proof. Heaven Hill, a family company in Bardstown, has long been one of the main keepers of the bonded style.
oldforester86-sb: George Garvin Brown, a Louisville pharmaceutical salesman, began selling Old Forester in 1870, presenting it as the first bourbon sold exclusively in sealed glass bottles, a guarantee against the tampering common at the time. The name is thought to honour Dr. William Forrester, a Louisville physician, though the second r was later dropped. Brown's firm became Brown-Forman, and Old Forester stayed on sale through Prohibition under one of the few licences to bottle whiskey for medicinal use, so the brand says it has been sold continuously by the same company since it began.
oldforester1920-sb: Old Forester dates from 1870, when George Garvin Brown began selling it in Louisville in sealed bottles, and it kept going through Prohibition under one of the few federal licences to bottle whiskey for medicinal use. The 1920 Prohibition Style, announced in 2016 as part of the Whiskey Row Series, is bottled at 115 proof, meant to evoke the robust bourbon the company sold on doctors' prescriptions in those years. The series retells the brand's history in chapters, each bottling named for a year in that history.
henrymckenna10bib-sb: Henry McKenna, who had emigrated from Ireland, is said to have begun distilling in Fairfield, Kentucky, in 1855, and his name outlived his distillery. The brand passed through several owners before Heaven Hill of Bardstown acquired it, and this version is a single barrel bourbon aged ten years and bottled in bond: from one distilling season, aged in a bonded warehouse and bottled at 100 proof. Each bottle is marked with its barrel number and the date the barrel was filled.
wildturkeylongbranch-sb: Longbranch arrived in 2018 as a collaboration between Wild Turkey and the actor Matthew McConaughey, who had become the brand's creative director in 2016. Developed with master distiller Eddie Russell, it is an eight-year-old Kentucky bourbon refined through charcoal from Texas mesquite and American oak, a nod to McConaughey's Texan roots alongside the brand's Kentucky home. Wild Turkey itself takes its name from a 1940 hunting trip on which an Austin Nichols executive shared the company's bourbon with friends.
larceny-sb: Heaven Hill launched Larceny in 2012 as a wheated bourbon, and its name comes from a story attached to John E. Fitzgerald, whose name lives on in the Old Fitzgerald brand. As the brand tells it, Fitzgerald was a treasury agent with keys to the bonded warehouses who helped himself to the choicest barrels. Old Fitzgerald was a wheated bourbon from the Stitzel-Weller distillery, and Heaven Hill acquired the brand in 1999, building Larceny on the same style of recipe with wheat in place of rye.
1792smallbatch-sb: This bourbon comes from the Barton distillery in Bardstown, Kentucky, which dates its founding to 1879 and was long associated with the Tom Moore name, and it takes its name from the year Kentucky became a state. It began life as Ridgewood Reserve 1792, became 1792 Ridgemont Reserve after a trademark dispute, and later settled on 1792 Small Batch. The Sazerac Company, which bought the distillery in 2009, renamed it the Barton 1792 Distillery after the bourbon.
bulleitbourbon-sb: Tom Bulleit, a Louisville lawyer, started the Bulleit brand in 1987, saying he was reviving a high-rye recipe of his great-great-grandfather Augustus Bulleit, a tavern keeper who, according to the family's account, made whiskey from around 1830 until his death in 1860. The bourbon was distilled under contract at first; Seagram bought the brand in 1997, and it passed to Diageo, which opened its own Bulleit distillery near Shelbyville, Kentucky, in 2017.
bulleitrye-sb: Bulleit Rye followed the brand's bourbon in 2011, a whiskey of 95 percent rye and 5 percent malted barley distilled by MGP in Lawrenceburg, Indiana, a major source of high-rye whiskey for American brands. It shares the squat, frontier-style bottle of the bourbon, with a green label. The Bulleit name goes back to Tom Bulleit, a Louisville lawyer who founded the brand in 1987 on a family recipe story, and the whiskey now belongs to Diageo.
rittenhouseryebib-sb: Rittenhouse Rye takes its name from Rittenhouse Square in Philadelphia and belongs to the Pennsylvania tradition of rye whiskey that dominated early American distilling. It first appeared after Prohibition, and when the Pennsylvania distilleries closed the brand passed to Heaven Hill, which makes it in Kentucky. Bottled in bond at 100 proof, it was one of the few ryes still widely available when bartenders rediscovered classic cocktails, and it became a familiar bottle for the Manhattan and the Sazerac.
sazeracrye-sb: The Sazerac Company gives 1850 as its founding year and takes its name from the Sazerac Coffee House in New Orleans, which served Sazerac-de-Forge et Fils cognac. The house cocktail was first made with that cognac, and the usual story says rye took its place in the late nineteenth century, when phylloxera cut supplies of French brandy. Sazerac Rye, made at the company's Buffalo Trace Distillery in Frankfort, Kentucky, is named after that drink, and an older version, Sazerac 18, appears in the Buffalo Trace Antique Collection.
whistlepig10rye-sb: WhistlePig was launched in 2010 by Raj Bhakta, who had bought a farm in Shoreham, Vermont, a few years earlier. Its first whiskey was a ten-year-old, 100 percent rye sourced from Alberta Distillers in Canada, chosen with the help of the master distiller Dave Pickerell, formerly of Maker's Mark, and bottled in Vermont. Whistle pig is an old country name for the groundhog, and the company later began distilling its own rye on the farm.
whistlepig12oldworld-sb: WhistlePig, launched in 2010 from a farm in Shoreham, Vermont, built its name on aged rye whiskey sourced from Canada and finished at the farm. The 12-year Old World takes its name from its European wine casks: the rye is finished in barrels that once held Madeira, Sauternes and port, and the finishes are blended together. The company's founding master distiller, Dave Pickerell, formerly of Maker's Mark, helped design its early releases before his death in 2018.
michtersus1rye-sb: The Michter's name was coined in the 1950s by Louis Forman, who owned an old distillery at Schaefferstown, Pennsylvania, and named his whiskey after his sons Michael and Peter. That distillery traced its origins to 1753, when the Swiss Mennonite farmer John Shenk began distilling rye there, and it closed after a bankruptcy in 1989. Chatham Imports later revived the name, and Michter's whiskeys have been made in Kentucky since the 2000s, with the company opening its own distillery in Shively. US*1 is its core range.
michtersus1bourbon-sb: Michter's takes its name from a whiskey Louis Forman created in the 1950s at the Bomberger's distillery in Schaefferstown, Pennsylvania, combining the names of his sons Michael and Peter. That historic distillery, whose roots go back to 1753, closed in 1989, and Chatham Imports later revived the name for whiskeys made in Kentucky. The US*1 Bourbon is the core small batch bourbon of the range, and the company now distils in Shively and at the restored Fort Nelson Building on Louisville's Whiskey Row.
highwestdoublerye-sb: High West opened in Park City, Utah, in 2007 as the state's first licensed distillery since Prohibition, founded by David Perkins, a former biochemist, and his wife Jane. Perkins made his name blending whiskeys from other distilleries, and Double Rye does what its name says, marrying two rye whiskeys of different ages and recipes, one young and spicy, one older and rounder. The company runs a saloon in a former livery stable and garage in Park City, and Constellation Brands bought it in 2016.
highwestrendezvousrye-sb: Rendezvous Rye was among the first releases of High West, which David and Jane Perkins opened in Park City, Utah, in 2007 as the state's first licensed distillery since Prohibition. The whiskey blends older and younger straight ryes sourced from other distilleries, and its name recalls the rendezvous of the Rocky Mountain fur trade, the summer gatherings where trappers met traders. High West, now part of Constellation Brands, has since added whiskey from its own stills in Utah.
pikesvillerye-sb: Pikesville Rye takes its name from Pikesville, Maryland, outside Baltimore, and is one of the last survivors of the Maryland rye style, once a rival to Pennsylvania's in American bars. After Prohibition the brand passed through Maryland producers before Heaven Hill acquired it and moved production to Kentucky. Heaven Hill later relaunched it as a six-year-old bottled at 110 proof, a much stronger whiskey than the version long sold around Baltimore.
oldoverholt-sb: Old Overholt is dated to 1810, when Abraham Overholt took over his family's farm distillery at West Overton, Pennsylvania, and made it into a business. His grandson, the industrialist Henry Clay Frick, later became a partner along with Andrew Mellon, and the whiskey carried the Old Overholt name with Abraham's stern portrait on the label. A medicinal whiskey permit carried the brand through Prohibition, and it is often called America's oldest continuously maintained whiskey brand. Beam has made it in Kentucky since 1987.
templetonrye-sb: The modern Templeton Rye was introduced in 2006, drawing on the story of the bootleg rye made by farmers around Templeton, Iowa, during Prohibition, which local lore says was a favourite of Al Capone. For years the whiskey was distilled in Lawrenceburg, Indiana, by MGP, and after a class-action settlement in 2015 the labels were changed to say so and to drop claims about a Prohibition-era recipe. The company has since built its own distillery in Templeton to make the whiskey in Iowa.
jackdanielsoldno7-sb: Jack Daniel's labels say the distillery was established and registered in 1866 in Lynchburg, Tennessee, though Daniel's biographer argues the business was not registered until 1875. Jasper Newton 'Jack' Daniel learned to distil from the preacher Dan Call and from Nathan 'Nearest' Green, an enslaved man who became the distillery's first master distiller after emancipation. The whiskey is filtered through sugar maple charcoal, the Lincoln County Process. Why it is called Old No. 7 remains unclear, and Brown-Forman has owned the company since 1956.
jackdanielssinglebarrel-sb: Jack Daniel's Single Barrel was introduced in 1997, the first Jack Daniel's sold barrel by barrel, and it is bottled at 94 proof. Barrels for it are chosen from those maturing high in the barrelhouses, where temperature swings are greatest, and each bottle carries its barrel number. The distillery itself dates from the 1860s or 1870s in Lynchburg, Tennessee, where Jack Daniel learned his craft from Nathan 'Nearest' Green.
gentlemanjack-sb: Gentleman Jack was introduced in 1988, billed as the first new whiskey from Jack Daniel's in more than a century, and it is charcoal mellowed twice: once before ageing, as all Jack Daniel's is, and again after it leaves the barrel. The name nods to Jack Daniel himself, remembered as a dapper figure in a planter's hat and knee-length coat. The whiskey is made at the Lynchburg distillery in Tennessee, which Brown-Forman has owned since 1956.
georgedickelno12-sb: Schenley first bottled George Dickel Tennessee Whisky in 1964, from a distillery Ralph Dupps had rebuilt at Cascade Hollow near Tullahoma, close to where Cascade whisky was made in the nineteenth century. George A. Dickel, a German-born Nashville merchant, had sold that Cascade whisky, and the brand keeps the Scottish spelling, whisky without an e. The spirit is chilled before it is filtered through sugar maple charcoal, a Dickel signature, and the distillery now belongs to Diageo.
unclenearest1856-sb: Fawn Weaver launched Uncle Nearest in 2017 to honour Nathan 'Nearest' Green, an enslaved man who taught the young Jack Daniel to distil and became Jack Daniel's first master distiller after emancipation. Weaver set out to document his story after reading about him in a 2016 New York Times article, and Victoria Eady Butler, Green's great-great-granddaughter, became the brand's master blender. The 1856 bottling is one of its premium aged whiskeys, and the company opened its own Nearest Green Distillery in Shelbyville, Tennessee.
balconestexassinglemalt-sb: Chip Tate founded Balcones Distilling in Waco, Texas, in 2008, building stills by hand in a former welding shop beneath a bridge, and named it after the Balcones Escarpment, the fault line that crosses central Texas. Texas Single Malt became one of its core whiskies, matured in a climate whose summer heat works the casks hard. Tate left the company in 2014, and Balcones has since moved into a larger distillery in downtown Waco, where Texas Single Malt is still made.
westwardamericansinglemalt-sb: Westward grew out of House Spirits, a Portland, Oregon, distillery co-founded in 2004 by Christian Krogstad, who wanted to make a single malt with the brewing character of the Pacific Northwest. The whiskey is fermented with ale yeast from a wash of two-row barley grown in the region, double pot distilled and aged in new charred American oak, borrowing equally from craft beer and Scotch. The company later renamed itself after the whiskey to concentrate on it.
stranahansbluepeak-sb: Stranahan's was founded in Denver in 2004 by Jess Graber and George Stranahan, who, as the story goes, met when Graber, a volunteer firefighter, came to put out a fire at Stranahan's barn. Stranahan also co-founded the Flying Dog brewery, and the distillery drew on brewing know-how to make an early American single malt from Colorado barley. Blue Peak is finished in a solera system that keeps older whiskey in the vat as new batches are added.
westlandamericanoak-sb: Westland Distillery was founded in Seattle in 2010 by Emerson Lamb, with distiller Matt Hofmann, to make a single malt that reflected the Pacific Northwest, from its barley to its climate. Westland builds its whiskey from several malts, including darker brewer's malts, and American Oak, its flagship, is matured largely in new American oak casks. Rémy Cointreau bought the distillery in 2016, and Westland has campaigned for American single malt to be recognised as a category in its own right.
mccarthysoregonsinglemalt-sb: Steve McCarthy founded Clear Creek Distillery in Portland, Oregon, in 1985, using fruit from his family's Hood River orchards to make European-style eaux-de-vie. He went on to make an Islay-style whiskey: McCarthy's Oregon Single Malt, made from peated barley imported from Scotland and aged partly in Oregon oak, became one of the early single malts of the American craft era. Hood River Distillers bought Clear Creek in 2014 and continues the whiskey.
mellowcorn-sb: Mellow Corn is a rare bottled-in-bond corn whiskey, made by Heaven Hill, the Bardstown, Kentucky, family company founded in 1935. Corn whiskey descends from the frontier spirits of early American settlers: by law it must be at least 80 percent corn, and when aged it goes into used or uncharred barrels, which keep it paler and closer to the grain. As a bonded whiskey it is aged at least four years, comes from a single distilling season and is bottled at 100 proof.
balconesbabyblue-sb: Baby Blue was the first whisky released by Balcones Distilling, which Chip Tate founded in Waco, Texas, in 2008, and the distillery presented it as the first Texas whisky sold since Prohibition. It is made from roasted Hopi blue corn in the form of atole, the toasted corn meal of the American Southwest, which gives it a nutty, toasty character. Balcones takes its name from the Balcones Escarpment, the fault line that runs across central Texas past Waco.
bernheimoriginalwheat-sb: Heaven Hill introduced Bernheim Original in 2005 as a straight wheat whiskey, with winter wheat as its main grain, a style hardly seen on American shelves at the time. It is named after Isaac Wolfe Bernheim, a German immigrant who built a whiskey business in Louisville in the late nineteenth century and created the I. W. Harper brand. Heaven Hill had bought the Bernheim distillery in Louisville in 1999 and makes its whiskeys there, including this one.
fireball-sb: Fireball was developed by Seagram in the mid-1980s as one of a line of flavoured spirits, originally sold as Dr. McGillicuddy's Fireball Whisky and built on Canadian whisky. The Sazerac Company of New Orleans bought the brand and recipe in 1989, and in 2007 gave it its present name and look as Fireball Cinnamon Whisky. Its flavour recalls the hard cinnamon candies known as fireballs, and the brand remains part of the Sazerac portfolio.
skrewballpeanutbutterwhiskey-sb: Skrewball was launched in 2018 in San Diego by Steven Yeng and his wife Brittany Merrill Yeng. Steven, a restaurant and bar owner, had created a peanut butter flavoured whiskey drink for his bar, and its local following led the couple to bottle a peanut butter whiskey of their own. It is widely credited with popularising peanut butter whiskey as a category, and Pernod Ricard took a majority stake in the company in 2023.
olesmokymoonshine-sb: Ole Smoky opened in 2010 in Gatlinburg, Tennessee, after a change in state law allowed distilleries in many more counties, and presented itself as the first federally licensed distillery in the history of East Tennessee. Its founders set out to bottle the moonshine tradition of the Great Smoky Mountains, where families had long made unaged corn whiskey out of sight of the revenue men, and sold it in mason jars. Its jars and flavoured moonshines helped popularise legal moonshine across the country.
midnightmoon-sb: Midnight Moon was launched in 2007 by Piedmont Distillers of Madison, North Carolina, in partnership with Junior Johnson, the NASCAR driver and team owner who grew up in a moonshining family in Wilkes County. Johnson, who had hauled his family's whiskey as a young man, became a part-owner of the distillery, and the moonshine was presented as a nod to that family tradition, made in small batches from corn. Piedmont, billed as North Carolina's first legal distillery since Prohibition, worked from the town's old train depot.
crownroyal-sb: Samuel Bronfman of Seagram created Crown Royal in 1939 as a tribute to King George VI and Queen Elizabeth, whose royal tour of Canada that year was the first by a reigning monarch. The whisky came in a bottle shaped to suggest a crown, inside a purple bag with a gold drawstring, and for years it was sold mainly in Canada before it spread abroad in the 1960s. It is made at Gimli, Manitoba, on the shore of Lake Winnipeg, and now belongs to Diageo.
crownroyalnorthernharvestrye-sb: Crown Royal was created by Seagram in 1939 to mark the royal tour of King George VI and Queen Elizabeth, and Northern Harvest Rye is one of its later additions, a blended Canadian whisky made with a mash of 90 percent rye. The grain comes from the Canadian prairies and the whisky is made at Crown Royal's distillery at Gimli, on Lake Winnipeg in Manitoba. It brought fresh attention to genuine rye in Canadian whisky, where the word has long been used loosely for blends of any grain.
canadianclub-sb: Hiram Walker, a Detroit grocer and grain merchant, opened a distillery across the river in Windsor, Ontario, in 1858 and built a company town around it, Walkerville. His whisky became popular in gentlemen's clubs and was sold as Club Whisky; when American distillers pressed for its foreign origin to be made clear, Walker added 'Canadian' to the label in 1889, a change said to have only added to its appeal. Canadian Club received a royal warrant from Queen Victoria and now belongs to Suntory Global Spirits.
albertapremium-sb: Alberta Distillers was founded in Calgary in 1946 by the oilman Frank McMahon and the newspaper publisher Max Bell. It specialises in whisky made entirely from Canadian prairie rye, unusual even in Canada, and Alberta Premium became its flagship. The distillery also supplies aged rye to other brands, including the whiskey behind WhistlePig's first releases, and belongs to Suntory Global Spirits.
lotno40-sb: Lot No. 40 was first released in 1998 by Hiram Walker in Windsor, Ontario, a whisky made from 100 percent rye in a copper pot still, in the manner of early Canadian settler distillers. It found little market at first and was discontinued, then revived in 2012 by Corby, the Canadian arm of Pernod Ricard, under master blender Don Livermore. Its name, the brand says, comes from a numbered land lot in early Upper Canada where a settler once distilled.
fortycreekbarrelselect-sb: John K. Hall, a winemaker, took over the Kittling Ridge winery and distillery at Grimsby, Ontario, in 1992 and set about making whisky with a winemaker's approach, distilling rye, barley and corn separately and ageing each before blending, much like a meritage wine. His whiskies came to market under the name Forty Creek, after Forty Mile Creek, which flows through Grimsby into Lake Ontario. Barrel Select became the flagship, and Campari bought the company in 2014.
jpwisersdeluxe-sb: John Philip Wiser, a young American from New York State, came to Prescott, Ontario, on the St Lawrence River in 1857 and went on to own the local distillery, building it into one of Canada's notable whisky businesses. The brand later passed through several hands and came to be made at the Hiram Walker distillery in Windsor, Ontario. It now belongs to Corby, part of Pernod Ricard, and Deluxe has long been its mainstay blend.
yamazaki12-sb: Suntory released Yamazaki 12 in 1984, presenting it as Japan's first single malt, from the distillery Shinjiro Torii had founded in 1923 at Yamazaki, between Kyoto and Osaka, where three rivers meet and mist gathers. Yamazaki was Japan's first commercial whisky distillery, and Masataka Taketsuru, who had studied whisky making in Scotland, served as its first manager. The 12-year-old helped introduce Japanese single malt to drinkers abroad.
yamazaki18-sb: Shinjiro Torii founded the Yamazaki distillery in 1923 in the hills between Kyoto and Osaka, Japan's first commercial whisky distillery, with Masataka Taketsuru as its first manager. The site was chosen for its soft water and humid climate at the meeting of three rivers. Yamazaki 18 is the distillery's long-aged single malt, including whisky matured in casks of Japanese mizunara oak, a wood Suntory turned to, the story goes, when imported casks were scarce. Demand for aged Japanese whisky has made it hard to find in recent years.
hakushu12-sb: Suntory built its Hakushu distillery in 1973 in the forests on the slopes of Mount Kaikoma in Yamanashi Prefecture, in the Japanese Southern Alps, half a century after it had opened Yamazaki. The high, wooded setting and soft mountain water suit the fresh, often lightly smoky style of its malts, and the 12-year-old became Hakushu's signature single malt. Hakushu is also a key component of Suntory's Hibiki and Toki blends.
hibikiharmony-sb: Japanese Harmony joined the Hibiki range in 2015, a no-age-statement blend introduced as stocks of older Japanese whisky ran short. Suntory's Hibiki line had begun in 1989, marking the company's ninetieth anniversary, and Harmony blends malt and grain whiskies from the Yamazaki, Hakushu and Chita distilleries. Hibiki means resonance, and the bottle's 24 facets represent the 24 seasons of the traditional Japanese calendar.
hibiki17-sb: Hibiki was introduced in 1989 to mark the ninetieth anniversary of Suntory, which Shinjiro Torii founded as a wine shop in Osaka in 1899, and the 17-year-old was among its earliest expressions. The blend brings together malts from Yamazaki and Hakushu with grain whisky from Chita, and its name means resonance. Hibiki 17 became known abroad after appearing in Sofia Coppola's film Lost in Translation, and it was later withdrawn as stocks of aged whisky ran short.
nikkafromthebarrel-sb: Nikka introduced From The Barrel in 1985, a blend of malt and grain whiskies that is married again in casks after blending and bottled at 51.4 percent, stronger than most blends. Its small, square bottle is meant to suggest a solid block of whisky. Nikka itself was founded in 1934 by Masataka Taketsuru, who had studied whisky making in Scotland, and the blend draws on the company's Yoichi and Miyagikyo distilleries.
nikkacoffeygrain-sb: Nikka installed a Coffey still imported from Scotland in 1963, a continuous still of the type patented by the Irish inventor Aeneas Coffey in 1830, and later moved it to its Miyagikyo distillery near Sendai. These old-fashioned column stills run slowly and keep more of the grain's flavour than modern ones, which Nikka's founder Masataka Taketsuru valued. Coffey Grain, made mainly from corn, bottles that grain whisky on its own rather than only as a blending component.
yoichisinglemalt-sb: Masataka Taketsuru founded Yoichi in 1934 on the coast of Hokkaido, choosing a cool, damp site that reminded him of Scotland, where he had studied chemistry and learned distilling. His company began as Dai Nippon Kaju, selling apple juice while the whisky matured, and later shortened its name to Nikka. Yoichi's pot stills are still heated directly with coal, an old method few distilleries keep, which helps give its malts their heavy, often smoky character.
miyagikyosinglemalt-sb: Nikka opened its second distillery, Miyagikyo, in 1969 in a valley near Sendai, where the Hirose and Nikkawa rivers meet. The story goes that Masataka Taketsuru, the company's founder, chose the site after mixing whisky with water from the Nikkawa and tasting it on the spot. Where Yoichi's malts are robust, Miyagikyo uses large steam-heated stills for a lighter, fruitier spirit, and the distillery also houses the company's Coffey stills.
chichibuichirosmalt-sb: Ichiro Akuto founded Venture Whisky in 2004, the year his family's company, owner of the shuttered Hanyu distillery, was sold; he saved its remaining casks and released them as Ichiro's Malt. He then built his own Chichibu distillery in the hills of Saitama Prefecture, which began distilling in 2008 as the first new whisky distillery licensed in Japan in decades. The first Chichibu single malt appeared in 2011, and the distillery has since become one of the most collected names in Japanese whisky.
marsiwaitradition-sb: Hombo Shuzo, a shochu maker from Kagoshima, opened a whisky distillery in Yamanashi in 1960 designed by Kiichiro Iwai, who had been Masataka Taketsuru's superior at Settsu Shuzo, the company that sent Taketsuru to study in Scotland. Hombo moved its whisky making to the Mars Shinshu distillery in the Nagano Alps in 1985, and after a long pause restarted distilling there in 2011. Iwai Tradition, a blend, is named in Kiichiro Iwai's honour.
suntorytoki-sb: Suntory introduced Toki in 2016, first in the United States, as a blend designed for mixing, especially in the highball that Japanese bars have long served. It brings together malt from Hakushu and Yamazaki with grain whisky from the Chita distillery. Toki means time in Japanese, a name Suntory ties to the joining of old and new in its whisky making, which began when Shinjiro Torii opened Yamazaki in 1923.
amrutfusion-sb: Amrut Distilleries was founded in Bangalore in 1948 by J. N. Radhakrishna Rao Jagdale, and for decades it made spirits for the Indian market. In 2004 it launched a single malt in Scotland, an unusual step for an Indian distiller, and Fusion followed, combining malt from Indian barley with malt from peated Scottish barley, bottled at 50 percent. Its reception abroad helped change how many whisky drinkers saw Indian single malt. Amrut takes its name from amrit, the Sanskrit word for the nectar of the gods.
pauljohnbrilliance-sb: Paul P. John founded John Distilleries in 1992, and the company grew on mass-market Indian whisky before building a malt distillery in Goa. Its first single malt was launched in London in 2012, and Brilliance became one of its flagship bottlings: an unpeated malt made from Indian six-row barley and matured in American oak in Goa's tropical heat, which speeds the interaction with the wood.
rampurdoublecask-sb: The Rampur distillery in Uttar Pradesh dates from 1943 and is run by Radico Khaitan, which built a business on mass-market Indian spirits before releasing Rampur Indian Single Malt in 2016. The name comes from the former princely state of Rampur, on the plains below the Himalayan foothills, whose extremes of summer heat and monsoon humidity make for quick maturation. Double Cask marries malts aged in American oak and in European oak casks.
indritrini-sb: Indri single malt was launched in 2021 by Piccadily Agro Industries, from a distillery at the village of Indri in Haryana, north of Delhi, and made with Indian six-row barley. Trini, the debut expression, takes its name from its three woods: ex-bourbon, ex-French wine and Pedro Ximénez sherry casks, matured through hot summers and cool winters. Its quick success abroad made Indri one of the most talked-about new names in Indian whisky.
mcdowellsno1-sb: McDowell's takes its name from McDowell and Co., set up in British India by the Scottish trader Angus McDowell in the nineteenth century. The company passed into Indian hands in the middle of the twentieth century and became the core of the UB Group's spirits business, now United Spirits, part of Diageo. Like most Indian whisky, McDowell's No.1 is a blend built largely on spirit distilled from molasses, and it grew into one of the best-known whisky names in India.
officerschoice-sb: Officer's Choice was launched in 1988 by the company now called Allied Blenders and Distillers, founded by Kishore Chhabria. It was aimed at affordable, everyday Indian whisky, with a name that carries a military ring, and it grew into one of the most widely sold whisky brands in India. Later bottlings such as Officer's Choice Black added imported Scotch malts to the blend.
royalstag-sb: Seagram launched Royal Stag in India in 1995, blending grain spirit with imported Scotch malts, a departure from the molasses-based spirit behind most Indian whisky at the time. Pernod Ricard took over the brand when it bought Seagram's drinks business in 2001, and Royal Stag grew into one of India's best-known whiskies.
kavalanclassic-sb: Kavalan is the whisky of the King Car Group, a Taiwanese food and drinks company, which built its distillery in Yuanshan, Yilan County, in 2005 and ran its first spirit in 2006. Kavalan Classic, the first release, appeared in 2008. The name is the old name for Yilan, taken from the Kavalan people, and the subtropical climate between the sea and the mountains makes the whisky mature much faster than it would in Scotland.
kavalansolistsherry-sb: Kavalan's distillery in Yilan County, Taiwan, was built by the King Car Group in 2005, and its Solist range of single cask, cask strength whiskies brought it international attention. Solist, a name that suggests a soloist, bottles single casks at full strength, and the sherry versions are matured in Spanish casks that once held sherry. Taiwan's heat and humidity draw flavour from the wood quickly, so these whiskies are bottled young by Scottish standards. Kavalan is the old name for Yilan.
omarsinglemalt-sb: Omar is the single malt range of the Taiwan Tobacco and Liquor Corporation, the former state monopoly, made at its Nantou distillery in central Taiwan, which began making malt whisky in 2008. Nantou had long produced fruit wines and other drinks, and its whiskies are matured in a range of casks, including bourbon and sherry, with some finished in casks that held Taiwanese fruit liqueurs.
theenglishoriginal-sb: The English Whisky Company began distilling in 2006 at St George's Distillery in Roudham, Norfolk, founded by James Nelstrop and his son Andrew and billed as the first dedicated whisky distillery in England for more than a century. Norfolk was chosen for its barley-growing country, and the company recruited Iain Henderson, formerly of Laphroaig, to set up production. The Original is its straightforward, unpeated single malt.
cotswoldssinglemalt-sb: Dan Szor, a New Yorker who had worked in finance, founded the Cotswolds Distillery in 2014 at Stourton, near Shipston-on-Stour in Warwickshire, on the northern edge of the Cotswolds. He wanted to make whisky from local barley, and the first single malt was released in 2017, after the distillery had made gin while its whisky matured. Its single malts are known for a rich, fruity style, shaped partly by casks that once held red wine.
bimbersinglemalt-sb: Bimber was founded in 2015 by Dariusz Plazewski, a Pole whose family, the story goes, had made spirits at home for generations, and set up in an industrial unit in Park Royal, west London. Bimber is the Polish word for home-made moonshine, a nod to that tradition. The distillery malts its own barley on the floor, ferments slowly and distils in small copper stills, and its first single malt, released in 2019, drew wide interest among collectors.
penderynmadeira-sb: Penderyn began distilling in 2000 at the village of Penderyn on the edge of the Brecon Beacons, and when its first whisky went on sale in 2004 it was the first commercially made in Wales for more than a century. The distillery uses a distinctive copper still designed by David Faraday that produces a light, high-strength spirit. Its Madeira expression, matured in ex-bourbon barrels and finished in Madeira wine casks, became the house's signature.
mhclassic-sb: Milk & Honey was founded in 2012 in Tel Aviv-Jaffa, taking its name from the biblical description of the land as one flowing with milk and honey. The distillery worked with the late Scottish whisky consultant Jim Swan, and Tel Aviv's heat and humidity mature its spirit quickly. Classic, matured mainly in ex-bourbon casks with some red wine casks, is the house single malt, and the distillery also ages casks by the Dead Sea, the lowest place on land.
starwardnova-sb: David Vitale founded Starward in Melbourne in 2007, setting out to make a whisky that reflected Australia rather than imitating Scotland. The distillery leaned on the country's wine industry, maturing its single malt in barrels that had held Australian red wine, and moved from its first home at Essendon Fields to a larger site in Port Melbourne. Nova, aged entirely in red wine barrels such as shiraz, cabernet and pinot noir, became its flagship, and Diageo's Distill Ventures invested in the business.
sullivanscovefrenchoak-sb: Sullivans Cove whisky began in 1994 at the Tasmania Distillery in Hobart, named after the cove on the Derwent River where the city was founded in 1804. Tasmania had a long history of distilling before it was outlawed in the colonial era, and the island's modern revival was then only just beginning. The distillery's small, single cask releases of Tasmanian barley malt drew international attention, and the French Oak expression is matured in French oak casks that once held Australian fortified wine.
larkclassiccask-sb: Bill Lark, a surveyor, and his wife Lyn founded Lark Distillery in Hobart in 1992, after persuading the authorities to license a small still, something rules dating from the early twentieth century had made impossible in Tasmania. Their success opened the way for the island's modern whisky industry, and Bill Lark is often called the godfather of Tasmanian whisky. Classic Cask is the distillery's core single malt, made from Tasmanian barley and matured in casks that once held Australian fortified wine.
thomsonsouthisland-sb: Thomson South Island comes from Thomson Whisky, a small independent New Zealand whisky maker, and its name points to the country's South Island, home of the Canterbury Plains and much of its barley growing.
brennefrenchsinglemalt-sb: Brenne was launched in 2012 by Allison Patel, an American and former professional ballet dancer, who found her whisky in the Cognac region of France. It is made by a farming family that grows its own barley and distils it twice in a traditional cognac alembic still, then ages it in new Limousin oak before finishing it in casks that once held cognac. Patel presented it as proof that France, better known for brandy and wine, could make a single malt with its own accent.
armorikclassic-sb: Armorik was launched in 1998 by Distillerie Warenghem of Lannion, in Brittany, and is billed as the first single malt made in the region. The firm was founded in 1900 by Léon Warenghem, who made liqueurs, including the herbal Elixir d'Armorique, and began making whisky in the 1980s. The name comes from Armorica, the ancient name for the Breton coast, and the whisky is double distilled in pot stills at Lannion.
mackmyrasvenskek-sb: Mackmyra was founded in 1999 by eight friends who had hit on the idea of a Swedish whisky during a ski trip the winter before, and it began distilling at the old Mackmyra mill near Gävle. The first release, Preludium 01, came out in 2006, and the company later built a tall gravity distillery nearby. Svensk Ek means Swedish oak: this single malt is matured in casks made from oak grown in Sweden, in keeping with Mackmyra's aim of making whisky from Swedish ingredients.
highcoasttimmer-sb: High Coast Distillery was founded in 2010 at Bjärtrå, on the Ångerman River in northern Sweden, and was first known as Box Destilleri before taking its present name. The name refers to the High Coast, a UNESCO World Heritage landscape on the Gulf of Bothnia shaped by the land rising after the last ice age. Timmer, Swedish for timber, is one of its peated single malts.
stauningrye-sb: Stauning was founded in 2005 by nine friends in the village of Stauning in West Jutland, who set out to make whisky from Danish grain using traditional methods. They malt their own barley and rye on the floor, and rye whisky became one of the distillery's signatures. Diageo's Distill Ventures invested in the company, which opened a larger distillery near the original site in 2018.
millstone10-sb: Zuidam Distillers was founded in 1975 by Fred van Zuidam at Baarle-Nassau, in the southern Netherlands, and is now run by his son Patrick. The family began distilling malt whisky in the late 1990s and called it Millstone, after the traditional Dutch windmills that grind its grain. The 10-year-old is one of the range's longer-aged single malts, and the distillery also makes genever and liqueurs in the Dutch tradition.
slyrsclassic-sb: Florian Stetter, a trained brewer and maltster, founded Slyrs in 1999 at Schliersee in the Bavarian Alps, an early pioneer of German single malt. The name comes from Slyrse, the old Bavarian name for the Schliersee lake and its monastery. The first release was small and sold locally, and the whisky is made from Bavarian barley, double distilled in copper pot stills and matured in new American oak.
reisetbauer12-sb: Hans Reisetbauer made his name with fruit brandies on his family farm near Linz in Upper Austria, and turned to whisky in the mid-1990s, using barley grown on his own land. His single malts are matured in casks that previously held Austrian sweet wines such as Trockenbeerenauslese, along with Chardonnay. The 12-year-old is one of the older bottlings in his range.
santismalt-sb: Säntis Malt comes from Brauerei Locher, a family brewery in Appenzell, Switzerland, which began making whisky in 1999, as soon as Swiss law allowed spirits to be distilled from grain. The brewery matured its malt in old oak beer casks, some of them more than a century old, giving it a character unlike most whiskies. The name comes from the Säntis, the highest peak in the Alpstein range above Appenzell.
hammerhead23-sb: Hammer Head began with a stock of single malt distilled in 1989 at the Prádlo distillery near Plzeň, part of the Czech spirits firm Stock, in the last months of Czechoslovakia's communist era. After the Velvet Revolution the casks were left largely undisturbed, the story goes, until the whisky was rediscovered and first released in 2011 as a 20-year-old. The 23-year-old is a later release from the same stock, made from Czech barley and matured in Czech oak.
murreeclassicmalt-sb: Murree Brewery was founded in 1860 at Ghora Gali, near the hill station of Murree, to supply beer to British troops, and later brewed at Rawalpindi. Since the 1940s it has been controlled by the Parsi Bhandara family, and it added whisky to its range, maturing malt in Pakistan. Alcohol has been prohibited for Muslims in Pakistan since 1977, so Murree sells mainly to non-Muslims and foreigners, and it remains one of very few legal distillers in the Muslim world.
kione-sb: Ki One is the single malt of Three Societies, a distillery opened in Namyangju, north-east of Seoul, by the Korean-American entrepreneur Bryan Do, and it is among the first single malts made in South Korea. Korea's distilling tradition centres on soju, and whisky making there is a recent development. Ki One matures through hot, humid summers and freezing winters, a climate that works the casks hard.
tanqueraylondondry-sb: Charles Tanqueray began distilling gin in Bloomsbury, London, in 1830, as the London dry style was taking shape. His son Charles Waugh Tanqueray built up the business, which merged with Gordon's in 1898, and the gin's squat green bottle is often said to have been inspired by a cocktail shaker, though no one has proved it. Tanqueray became a favourite for the martini and the gin and tonic in America in the twentieth century, and today it is distilled at Cameronbridge in Fife.
tanqueraynoten-sb: Tanqueray No. Ten was introduced in 2000, made in a small pot still nicknamed Tiny Ten, the distillery's still number ten, which gave the gin its name. Unlike most gins it uses whole fresh citrus, grapefruit, orange and lime, alongside chamomile and the classic juniper and coriander. It belongs to the line begun by Charles Tanqueray, who started distilling in Bloomsbury, London, in 1830, and is now made at Cameronbridge in Fife.
beefeater-sb: In the early 1860s the pharmacist James Burrough bought a distillery in Chelsea, London, and began making gin and liqueurs. By 1876 his London dry gin had taken the name Beefeater, after the Yeomen Warders who guard the Tower of London. The firm moved to Kennington, south London, in 1958, and Beefeater is still distilled there, one of the few historic London gin houses still making gin in the city. Its botanicals are steeped in the spirit for a day before distillation.
beefeater24-sb: Beefeater 24 was created by Desmond Payne, Beefeater's master distiller, and released in the late 2000s as a more aromatic companion to the classic gin. To the brand's usual botanicals he added Japanese sencha, Chinese green tea and grapefruit peel. The 24 refers to the 24-hour steeping of the botanicals before distillation at Kennington, south London, where Beefeater has been made since 1958, and the brand itself dates from James Burrough's Chelsea distillery.
bombaysapphire-sb: Bombay Sapphire was launched in 1987 by the drinks group International Distillers and Vintners as a new premium version of Bombay Dry Gin, with ten botanicals and a pale blue bottle. The name joins the colonial-era association of gin with India and the Star of Bombay, a violet-blue sapphire. Its botanicals are vapour infused, held in baskets above the spirit rather than steeped in it, and since 2014 it has been made at Laverstoke Mill in Hampshire, a converted paper mill with glasshouses by Thomas Heatherwick.
bombayoriginaldry-sb: Bombay Dry Gin was introduced in 1960 by the American importer Allan Subin, who based it on a recipe the brand traces to 1761 and a Warrington distiller, Thomas Dakin. Its name evokes British India, where gin and tonic is said to have taken hold among colonial officers who drank quinine tonic, and Queen Victoria's portrait appears on the label. It uses eight botanicals, two fewer than the Bombay Sapphire that later grew out of it.
gordons-sb: Alexander Gordon, a Scot, opened a gin distillery in Southwark, London, in 1769, and moved it to Goswell Road in Clerkenwell in 1786. The boar's head on the label comes from the Gordon clan's arms, linked to a legend of a Gordon saving a Scottish king from a wild boar. In 1898 Gordon's merged with Tanqueray, and the gin went on to hold royal warrants and become one of the most familiar names in gin. It is now distilled at Cameronbridge in Fife.
sipsmithlondondry-sb: Sipsmith was founded in 2009 by Sam Galsworthy and Fairfax Hall, with the drinks historian Jared Brown as master distiller, and set up in a small building in Hammersmith, west London, with a copper pot still named Prudence. Licensing a still that small took a long negotiation with HM Revenue and Customs, and the brand presents itself as the first copper pot distillery to open in London in nearly two centuries. Beam Suntory took a controlling stake in 2016, and Sipsmith now distils in Chiswick.
sipsmithvjop-sb: Sipsmith was founded in London in 2009 by Sam Galsworthy and Fairfax Hall with the drinks historian Jared Brown, and V.J.O.P., short for very junipery over proof, is its high-strength gin in the navy strength tradition. It is bottled at 57.7 percent, and juniper is used more than once in its making to push the pine character to the front. The distillery's copper stills, starting with Prudence, are all given women's names.
plymouthnavystrength-sb: Plymouth Gin has been distilled at the Black Friars Distillery in Plymouth since 1793, in a building dating from 1431 that is reputed to have been a Dominican monastery, and local tradition says some of the Pilgrim Fathers stayed there before the Mayflower sailed in 1620. The port's naval links made Plymouth a long-standing supplier to the Royal Navy, and navy strength, at 57 percent, is usually explained by the old shipboard test: gunpowder soaked with gin of that strength would still ignite.
haymanslondondry-sb: Hayman's is run by descendants of James Burrough, the pharmacist who created Beefeater, and the family dates its gin making to 1863, when Burrough began distilling in Chelsea. When the Beefeater business left the family in 1987, Christopher Hayman, Burrough's great-grandson, stayed in the gin trade and later built the Hayman's range with his children. The family's London Dry Gin is made in the Victorian tradition and is now distilled in Balham, south London.
haymansoldtom-sb: Hayman's introduced its Old Tom Gin in 2007, when the sweeter, softer style that came before London dry had almost disappeared, giving bartenders back the gin of many Victorian cocktail recipes. The family behind it descends from James Burrough, creator of Beefeater. The Old Tom name is usually traced to the eighteenth century, when, the story goes, Captain Dudley Bradstreet sold gin through a slot beneath a sign of a cat, a tom, in a London street.
jensensoldtom-sb: Christian Jensen, a Dane working in London, set out in the early 2000s to recreate the style of older London gins, inspired, the story goes, by a bottle he tasted in a Tokyo bar. His Bermondsey Dry Gin came first, and the Old Tom followed, made to a nineteenth-century recipe with no added sugar, its sweetness coming from the botanicals instead. Originally made under contract, the gins are now distilled under a railway arch in Bermondsey, south-east London.
hendricks-sb: Hendrick's was launched in 1999 by William Grant & Sons, created by Lesley Gracie at the company's Girvan distillery on the Ayrshire coast of Scotland. Gracie blends spirit from two very different stills, a Bennett still and a Carter-Head still, and then adds essences of cucumber and Bulgarian rose, an unusual pairing that set it apart from classic London dry gins. With its dark apothecary-style bottle, it is often credited with helping to start the modern gin revival. The name is said to honour a gardener once employed by the Grant family.
hendrickslunar-sb: Hendrick's Lunar was released in 2021, one of a series of limited editions from master distiller Lesley Gracie, and was presented as a gin inspired by night and the moon. Like the original Hendrick's, launched in 1999, it is made at William Grant & Sons' Girvan distillery in Ayrshire, Scotland, from spirit drawn from two contrasting stills, a Bennett still and a Carter-Head.
thebotanist-sb: The Botanist was launched in 2010 by Bruichladdich, the Islay whisky distillery, and is distilled slowly in Ugly Betty, a Lomond still rescued from the closed Inverleven distillery. Its recipe adds 22 botanicals hand-foraged on Islay, among them heather, bog myrtle and sweet cicely, to nine classic gin aromatics, and the foraging was guided by the local botanists Richard and Mavis Gulliver. It was devised under Jim McEwan, then Bruichladdich's master distiller.
caorunn-sb: Caorunn was launched in 2009 at the Balmenach distillery in Cromdale, in Speyside, where gin master Simon Buley distils it with five Celtic botanicals: rowan berry, heather, bog myrtle, dandelion and Coul Blush apple. Caorunn is the Gaelic word for rowan berry. The botanicals are infused by vapour inside a copper berry chamber, and the gin, like the whisky distillery that makes it, belongs to Inver House Distillers.
edinburghgin-sb: Edinburgh Gin was launched in 2010 by Alex and Jane Nicol of the Spencerfield Spirit Company as a gin that would capture Scotland's capital and its countryside. Its botanicals include Scottish pine, heather and milk thistle, a nod to the thistle that is Scotland's emblem. The brand opened a small distillery in the city's West End and later moved its main production to a larger site in Leith, and Ian Macleod Distillers bought the business in 2016.
